info.title: OpenSteward
info.description:
Self-hosted integration aggregator. One REST API across nine verticals:
accounting, CRM, e-commerce, logistics, payments, docsign, projects,
customer-support, and inventory platforms.

## Null semantics

This API is an **aggregation boundary**: it normalises data from many upstream platforms but doesn't own most of the content. To preserve full information, **`null`, key-omitted, and a value (including `""` or `0`) are three distinct facts**:

- **Key omitted** — upstream did not supply this field. The adapter mapped no equivalent value.
- **`null`** — upstream explicitly returned null / cleared / not reported.
- **Value** (`""`, `0`, or any other) — upstream supplied exactly that value.

Adapters never coerce missing → `0` or `0` → `null`. If a canonical field is absent from a response, the upstream platform did not provide an equivalent value. The verbatim upstream payload is preserved on every top-level canonical resource — under `raw` for payments, docsign, projects, customer-support and inventory, and under `metadata` for accounting, CRM, ecommerce and logistics — so the original platform representation is recoverable. **Two verticals are opt-in.** On payments and accounting the payload is withheld unless the operator enables `data_store.raw_payload.payments` / `data_store.raw_payload.accounting`, because across those adapters it declares bank account numbers, IBANs and card numbers the canonical schema deliberately does not expose. Card security codes are never returned, on any setting. Monetary amounts are integer minor units (e.g. cents) — never floats — and follow the same three-state rule (`null` = not reported, `0` = reported as zero, key-omitted = no equivalent).

Status, type, and category enums always include an explicit `"unknown"` member for upstream values the adapter could not map onto the normalized set — they are surfaced rather than silently dropped.

## Authentication — three schemes

The spec exposes **three security schemes** (`ApiKeyAuth`, `OAuth2Bearer` and `AdminSecret`). The first two are interchangeable developer credentials for `/v1/*`; the third is the operator path. Pick by what you are.

### 1. `ApiKeyAuth` — Bearer dev key (`/v1/*`, `/connect/*`)

Tenant-scoped developer key minted from `Admin → API keys → Mint key` in the admin UI, or the `mint-api-key` CLI. Send as:

```
Authorization: Bearer osk_<tenant>_<random>
```

Each key carries a list of scopes. Vertical access uses a **two-axis model**: `vertical:<v>` (or `vertical:read`) for the *touch* axis, and `vertical:write` as a separate gate for any non-GET on `/v1/{vertical}/*`. The default mint preset (the recommended "Safe default" radio) checks every scope **except** `vertical:write`, so a freshly minted key reads everywhere but cannot push writes back to upstream platforms — important for self-hosted operators who carry regulatory liability for what gets written upstream. See [/guides/dev-api.md §3](/guides/dev-api.md#3-scopes) for the full scope table, examples, and a 403 response shape.

Every `/v1/*` resource request additionally requires `connection_id` (UUID) as a query parameter. The connection row carries its own `vertical`, `platform`, and OAuth credentials.

Connections are created by completing the OAuth flow at `/auth/{vertical}/{platform}/connect` (admin-tooling) or by sending an end-user a hosted Connect Link from `POST /v1/customers/{id}/connect-links`.

### 2. `OAuth2Bearer` — OIDC bearer token (`/v1/*`)

An alternative to the static key on exactly the same routes, for deployments whose service accounts already live in an identity provider. The operator registers an issuer (Keycloak, Auth0, Okta and Entra ID ship as presets; any issuer with an OpenID discovery document works), and a developer presents a token from it:

```
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6…
```

OpenSteward is only a resource server here: it verifies against the issuer's published public keys and never mints a token or holds a client secret. The token resolves to the **same scope vocabulary** as a dev key, so every scope rule above applies unchanged — a route needing `vertical:write` needs it identically.

Off by default. A JWT sent to a deployment that has not enabled it answers `403 OAUTH_DISABLED`; an `osk_` key sent to a deployment where the operator has turned keys off answers `403 API_KEYS_DISABLED`. Verification failures all answer `401 UNAUTHENTICATED` with one body, so the response cannot be used to enumerate the operator's service accounts.

### 3. `AdminSecret` — `X-Admin-Secret` header (`/admin/*`, `DELETE /auth/.../{connectionId}`)

Operator-only secret used for **bootstrap and inter-service auth**. Set via the `ADMIN_SECRET` env var on the integration-server. Routes that take it: platform enable/disable/config (`/admin/platforms/*`), cross-tenant connection inspection (`/admin/connections*`), single-connection revoke under `/auth/{vertical}/{platform}/{connectionId}` (DELETE), and the operator sync-jobs surface (`/admin/sync-jobs*`).

Send as `X-Admin-Secret: <value>`. **Never give this to an external integrator** — it spans every tenant and bypasses the scope system. Day-2 operator actions on `/v1/connections*` should already be done with a tenant-scoped Bearer dev key (`connections:write` scope).

> Why a separate scheme rather than a "super scope" on a dev key? Bootstrap. The very first API call to a fresh deployment happens before any user, JWT, or developer key exists; `ADMIN_SECRET` is the single env-var that makes the integration-server reachable from admin-api during boot.

When enabled, mints an `osk_test_…` key (plaintext returned once) bound to a fresh throwaway tenant: it works only on the no-egress `/test/v1/*` sandbox, expires after 7 days, and minting is IP-rate-limited (3/hour). post.summary: Connect via static API key (no OAuth)
post.description:
For platforms whose `auth_type` is `api_key` (or similar non-OAuth) — primarily logistics carriers (e.g. FedEx, UPS, Shippo) and a handful of CRM platforms. Stores the static credential and returns the new connection.

**When to use this vs the GET variant:** check the platform's `auth_type` in `/v1/platforms/{vertical}/{slug}`. `oauth2` → use `GET /auth/{vertical}/{platform}/connect` (browser redirect). `api_key` (or any other non-oauth value) → use this POST.

Adapters that haven't opted into the static-credential flow (no `exchangeCredentials()`) reject this with 404 — fall back to the OAuth GET path.

**Credential fields are the adapter's, not a fixed `api_key`.** Send them as `fields`, keyed by the names in `credentialFields()` — `GET /v1/platforms/{vertical}/{slug}` lists them. Some adapters take one token, others take `clientId` + `clientSecret` plus an account id. `api_key` is accepted as shorthand **only** where the adapter declares exactly one field (the carrier case); anything else answers 400 and names what it needs.

`tenant_id` is optional: omit it for admin-tooling connections (the connection lands with `ownerTenantId = null` and won't appear under `/v1/customers/{id}/connections`). Provide it when minting a connection that should belong to one of your tenants.

**Two credentials, deliberately unequal.** Send `X-Admin-Secret` and `tenant_id` is taken from the body, so an operator can provision for any tenant or for none. Send a tenant Bearer key carrying `connections:write` and it works too — but `tenant_id` comes from the KEY and the body’s value is ignored, which is what makes it safe to expose: a tenant can provision its own carriers headlessly and cannot reach another’s. Presenting a Bearer header selects the tenant path even if a secret is also present, so the narrower rule wins.

This route always requires a credential: an unauthenticated caller able to supply `tenant_id` could mint a connection owned by any tenant and route that tenant’s traffic through an upstream account the caller controls. End-user credential entry belongs on the Connect Link flow, which is scoped by a one-time session token.

**Scope.** A sync only fills the local cache and never writes upstream, so the touch axis alone is enough — `vertical:{vertical}` or `vertical:read`. `vertical:write` is NOT required.

If you do not need a callback, send an empty JSON object as the body. The body is optional, but an empty one is not: the server rejects a request that sets `Content-Type: application/json` and sends nothing with `400 Body cannot be empty when content-type is set to 'application/json'` — and this console, like most REST clients, always sets that header. So send `{}` (or omit both the body and the header):

```sh
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  "$BASE/v1/{vertical}/sync?connection_id=<uuid>" -d '{}'
```

A `callback_url` must be `https`, carry no embedded credentials, and must not resolve to a loopback, private or link-local address; it is validated when the job is enqueued (`400 INVALID_CALLBACK_URL`) and re-resolved immediately before the callback is sent.

**In the sandbox** (`/test/v1/{vertical}/sync`, test keys) the job lifecycle is simulated: it walks pending → running → completed over ~2s (`?fast=true` completes before the response returns), completion seeds a couple of fresh fixture rows per resource type so a re-poll sees new data, and `callback_url` is validated and stored but **never dialed** — the sandbox makes no outbound requests; poll `GET /sync/{jobId}` instead. ApiKeyAuth.description:
Tenant-scoped developer API key. Send as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`.

Mint a key via the admin UI (Admin → API keys → Mint key) or the CLI:
`pnpm --filter integration-server mint-api-key --tenant <id> [--label <label>]`.

Each key carries a list of scopes. **Vertical access uses a two-axis model**:
- *Touch axis* (always required): `*`, `vertical:<v>`, `vertical:read`, or `vertical:write` controls **which** verticals the key can see.
- *Verb axis* (only on POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE): `*` or `vertical:write` controls **whether** the key can mutate vertical data.

Customers / connections / connect-links use a flat `:read` / `:write` split. Common scopes:
- `*` — full access.
- `customers:read`, `customers:write`, `customers:read_pii` — customer management + PII reveal.
- `connections:read`, `connections:write` — list / mutate connections.
- `connect-links:write` — spawn hosted Connect Link sessions.
- `vertical:read` — GET on every `/v1/{vertical}/*`.
- `vertical:write` — required for any non-GET on `/v1/{vertical}/*`.
- `vertical:accounting` / `vertical:crm` / `vertical:ecommerce` / `vertical:logistics` / `vertical:payments` / `vertical:docsign` / `vertical:projects` / `vertical:customer-support` / `vertical:inventory` — touch-axis access to one specific vertical.

See [/guides/dev-api.md §3](/guides/dev-api.md#3-scopes) for the full scope reference, examples, and the "safe default" mint preset (everything except `vertical:write`).

A request without the required scope returns `403 INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE`.

OAuth2Bearer.description:
OIDC bearer token issued by an identity provider the operator has registered, accepted on the same `/v1/*` surface as `ApiKeyAuth`. Send as `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>`.

Off unless the operator has enabled it (`auth.dev_oauth_enabled`) and registered an issuer under Admin → OAuth clients. When it is off, a JWT is refused with `403 OAUTH_DISABLED`; when API keys are off, an `osk_` key is refused with `403 API_KEYS_DISABLED`.

Get the token from the operator's IdP — Keycloak, Auth0, Okta and Entra ID ship as presets, and any issuer publishing an OpenID discovery document works. OpenSteward only verifies: it never mints these tokens and holds no client secret.

The token resolves to the **same scope vocabulary** as a dev key — the two-axis vertical model, `customers:*`, `mcp:read` and the rest — so a route requiring `vertical:write` requires it identically here. Where those scopes come from is the operator's choice per issuer: from a registered client row, from the token's own scope claim, or from the row narrowed by the claim.

Every verification failure answers `401 UNAUTHENTICATED` with the same body, deliberately: distinguishing a bad signature from an unregistered client would enumerate the operator's service accounts. The reason is in the deployment's logs.

This scheme is not declared with a `tokenUrl`, because the spec is static and deterministic while the token endpoint differs per deployment. Ask the operator for their issuer and audience.

Operator-only secret for `/admin/*` and a small number of platform-management routes. **Distinct from a developer key** — never give the admin secret to an external integrator.

The value is the `ADMIN_SECRET` env var on the integration-server. Used for: enabling/disabling platforms, setting platform OAuth credentials, listing every adapter across verticals, deleting any connection by UUID. End-user / developer flows should use a Bearer dev key instead.

IdempotencyKeyParam.name: Idempotency-Key
IdempotencyKeyParam.description: Opaque client-generated token (UUIDv4 recommended). When supplied on POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE, the server caches the response for 24h keyed by `(tenant, method, route, key)`, once authentication and the license checks have let the request through. Retrying the same request (URL including query, and body) with the same key replays the original response (`Idempotency-Replayed: true`); reusing the key with a different URL or body returns `422` with `Idempotency-Key-Conflict: true`; a concurrent retry while the first is in-flight returns `409` with `Retry-After`. A refusal (`401`, `403`, `409`, `429`, or any `LICENSE_*` error) is never cached, so a retry is checked again.

ConnectionIdParam.name: connection_id
ConnectionIdParam.description: UUID of the stored connection to use. On the live surface it is returned by the OAuth callback (`GET /auth/{vertical}/{platform}/callback`) — store it against your end-user record and pass it on every `/v1/{vertical}/*` request. **In test mode**, get one from `GET /test/v1/connections` (one per vertical, deterministic — start there).

PageParam.name: page
PageParam.description: Page number, 1-based: page N starts after (N − 1) × `meta.limit` rows. A missing page, or one that is not a decimal number of at least 1, is the first page.

LimitParam.name: limit
LimitParam.description: Records per page, at most 500. On `/v1/{vertical}/*` lists it defaults to 100 and is also capped at the platform's page maximum where the adapter declares one; `meta.limit` reports the page size served.

UpdatedAfterParam.name: updated_after
UpdatedAfterParam.description: Only return records modified at or after this ISO 8601 timestamp. Filters on each record's `updatedAt`, which every entity returns — so the correct watermark for an incremental poll is `max(updatedAt)` across the records you just received, NOT your own clock at request time. Using your clock loses any record modified while the request was in flight; a safety margin re-fetches a window and is a guess in both directions. The boundary is INCLUSIVE, and some platforms compare at second granularity (Xero does), so passing back `max(updatedAt)` re-delivers the records at that timestamp. That is deliberate: skipping past them would silently drop anything modified in the same second. Make your consumer idempotent — upsert by `id` — rather than advancing the watermark to exclude them.

IsLiveParam.name: is_live
IsLiveParam.description: Set to `true` to bypass the local DB cache and fetch fresh from the upstream platform. Fresh result is still written back to cache. No-op in `passthrough` mode.

IncludePiiParam.name: include_pii
IncludePiiParam.description: When `true`, response `data.pii` is populated with the decrypted record. Requires the `customers:read_pii` scope.

XRequestId.description: Per-request trace id. Echoes the inbound `X-Request-Id` when supplied; otherwise the server generates one. Quote this when contacting support — every log line carries the same id under `requestId`.

XRateLimitLimit.description: Rate-limit ceiling for the current window (requests).

XRateLimitRemaining.description: Requests remaining in the current rate-limit window.

XRateLimitReset.description: Seconds until the rate-limit window resets.

IdempotencyReplayed.description: Present on cached replays of an `Idempotency-Key`-bearing request — value is always `true`. Absent on first execution.

IdempotencyKeyConflict.description: Present on the `422` response when the same `Idempotency-Key` is reused with a different request URL or body. Value is always `true`.

RetryAfter.description: Suggested backoff in seconds. Returned on `409 idempotency_in_flight` and on rate-limit-exceeded responses.

tags.name: Accounting

**Resources**

- `providers` — Static metadata about enabled accounting platforms.

- `invoices` — Customer invoices (accounts receivable). Full CRUD.
- `bills` — Supplier bills (accounts payable). Full CRUD.

- `transactions` — Bank/payment transactions. Read-only.
- `taxrates` — Tax rates. Read-only.
- `expenses` — Employee expenses. List, get, create.
- `creditmemos` — Credit notes. List, get, create.
- `quotes` — Quotes / estimates — a priced offer made before any obligation exists. List and get; read-only. Not an invoice: nothing is owed until a quote is accepted and converted, so there is no paid, balance or due-date arithmetic on this resource.
- `orders` — Generic orders — the union view across a platform's order-like documents. List, get, create. **On platforms that model no separate sales order (Fortnox), `orders` and `salesorders` read the SAME upstream resource** and will return the same records; `orders` adds a `type` discriminator. Do not sum both, or you will double-count. **Xero has no sales-order entity at all** — `salesorders` is not implemented there, and `orders` instead reads the same upstream resource as `purchaseorders`, tagged `type: PURCHASE`.
- `salesorders` — Sales orders. List, get, create. See the note on `orders`: where a platform has no distinct sales-order entity, this is a projection of the same upstream documents rather than a separate set. `purchaseorders` is always distinct.
- `purchaseorders` — Purchase orders. List, get, create. Always a distinct upstream resource, unlike the orders/salesorders pair.

tags.name: Sandbox
tags.description: The test-mode control surface. `/test/v1/*` serves synthetic data with an `osk_test_…` key — or a token from the deployment’s own **test issuer** (`/test/oidc`: discovery, JWKS, and `POST /token`, which trades a test key for an OIDC bearer) — and makes no outbound call to any platform. Sandbox-only routes here: self-serve keys (`POST /test/v1/keys`), connection discovery (`GET /test/v1/connections` — start there), data reset (`DELETE /test/v1/reset`), and the **mock OAuth ceremony** (`/test/v1/auth/{vertical}/sandbox/connect` → hosted authorize page or `?outcome=…` → `/callback` granting the derived connection id). The tenant control plane (customers, connections, events, webhook-subscriptions) and a curated platform catalog are served under `/test/v1` too, and every vertical resource route mirrors `/v1/*` — pick the sandbox entry in the Servers dropdown to try one. Sandbox connect links open a hosted mock picker/authorize/done journey (HTML pages, unpublished here — see the dev-api guide).
